E1:
Your role

You will shape the systems foundations of verifiable agent autonomy: infrastructure through which flexible, learning-based agents can take consequential actions under explicit commitments. The project aims to make these ideas usable beyond a single demonstration, enabling researchers to investigate different models, tools and interaction patterns on a common execution framework.

This is an opportunity for architectural ownership and technical leadership in an emerging research programme. You will influence how formal guarantees connect to real execution, which abstractions can support a reusable framework, and how others can build on the resulting system. As it matures, there will be scope to help guide the public reference implementation and its developer community.

Within PC2, your main focus will be the Airlock, the execution layer connecting an agent's proposed actions to the evidence required by its contract. The first phase will develop a reusable core library for contractual state, proof requests, execution decisions and recorded outcomes, with clear extension interfaces for new benchmarks, toolsets and agent workflows. You will work with formal-methods and empirical researchers to identify what should be shared and what belongs in environment-specific adapters.

A second phase will develop stronger execution guarantees, including sandboxing and isolation, controlled access to credentials and resources, attestation and recovery from failures. The initial architecture will define the interfaces and trust boundaries required for this subsequent hardening. You will choose technologies and shape research priorities with the team, establishing the testing, documentation and release practices that allow the infrastructure to be inspected and reused.

Your contribution to the field

Your contribution will be a reusable systems architecture for enforceable agent commitments, connecting formal reasoning to the execution of real tools. Through the Airlock's interfaces, reference implementation and experimental evidence, you will shape how agent developers integrate proof-gated behaviour across environments. The framework will provide a basis for independent implementations and further security research, with scope for technical leadership of a public project at the intersection of agent infrastructure and formal verification.

An initial research or development direction

An example starting point is to connect two contrasting tool environments through a common Airlock core and use their differences to test its abstractions, execution traces and failure handling. This establishes a basis for investigating how stronger isolation and attestation change the system's guarantees and costs.

Essential background

  • Substantial hands-on software and systems engineering experience, with evidence of architectural ownership of a reusable library, execution system or research platform.
  • Strong implementation, testing and debugging skills, including the ability to reason about state, interfaces and failure behaviour.
  • Ability to turn evolving research requirements into maintainable software and to explain architectural decisions to collaborators.
  • Relevant technical training or equivalent professional experience. A publication record or PhD is not a prerequisite for this engineering profile; formal appointment eligibility will be specified in the final call.

Additional relevant experience

  • Security engineering, isolation, sandboxing, distributed systems, credential management or attestation.
  • Agent runtimes, tool integrations, observability or reproducible experimental infrastructure.
  • Formal methods, dependent type theory, proof-checking interfaces, or experience maintaining an open-source project.

Candidates with depth in a relevant area and an interest in connecting it to others are encouraged to apply. Evidence of your contribution can include research papers, formal developments, substantial software or a clear account of technical work that cannot be shared publicly.

Research environment and development

Your primary supervisor will be Alessandro Rudi. PC2 is a joint effort involving PRAXIS at AI4I, the REAL team at Bocconi and STAMP at Inria. The role requires close collaboration with the other participating groups, including opportunities for extended visiting periods at their laboratories, bringing your work into close contact with complementary expertise in machine learning, formal methods and systems.

The position is based in Milan, Italy. Remote working arrangements can be agreed when working from another laboratory in the PC2 collaboration. The timing and practical arrangements for research visits will be discussed with you and the participating hosts.

Computational resources. The joint programme is supported by AI4I's HPC infrastructure: approximately 150 NVIDIA GPUs (80 Blackwell B200 and 68 Hopper H200) and 5 PB of storage for agentic AI training, testing and validation. Access for collaborative projects will be arranged through the participating teams.

Research development and leadership

You will be expected and supported to communicate substantial technical and research results through appropriate publications, technical reports and open research artifacts. You will formulate systems questions and experiments that guide the development of the framework. The programme offers opportunities to co-lead technical contributions, mentor collaborators through design and code review, and progressively take responsibility for the reference Airlock's public development. The balance between implementation, investigation and dissemination will be agreed with your supervisor.

Application materials

Please prepare:

  • Your CV, including relevant research or technical experience.
  • A short statement of fit and interests, explaining what attracts you to the role, the experience you would bring and directions you would be interested in exploring. A full research proposal is not required.
  • One or two representative contributions, such as papers, formal developments or software. Briefly explain your own contribution. An account of non-public work is welcome; a public repository is not required.

Submission instructions and the application deadline will be published here when the call is finalised.
E2:
Your role

You will advance the capabilities of agents that learn from reasoning, verification and interaction. The scientific objective is to develop models that become better at capturing requirements, constructing evidence and revising their decisions, while understanding whether these improvements transfer to unfamiliar contracts, tools and tasks. The role offers the opportunity to shape a model-development agenda at the intersection of agent learning and formal reasoning.

You will take technical and scientific ownership of model improvement, combining hands-on training with the freedom to propose methods and lead experimental studies. Working alongside postdoctoral researchers and formal-methods specialists, you will lead the investigation of learning processes and turn new methods into reproducible experiments. You will lead research contributions and reusable releases alongside sustained ownership of the learning infrastructure.

Within PC2, directions include fine-tuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and learning from iterative or recursive problem-solving processes. These processes include decomposing obligations, repairing failed proofs, refining contracts after counterexamples and changing plans after rejected actions. You will investigate how these processes generate training signals and datasets, and which approaches improve the capabilities that the programme needs.

You will own the training and evaluation infrastructure that makes these investigations repeatable, adapting methods and diagnosing failures in models and feedback mechanisms. A central question is how improvements on a checking signal relate to useful task completion and faithful intent capture: these outcomes should not be conflated. You will work with the relevant researchers to establish informative comparisons and held-out tests; prior expertise in formal methods is not required.

Your contribution to the field

Your contribution will advance learning methods that turn verification and iterative reasoning into stronger agent capabilities. You will develop and evaluate approaches that use feedback from proof repair, contract refinement and planning, establishing how their benefits transfer to unfamiliar tasks. Research methods, model releases and reproducible training systems will give your work an identifiable place at the intersection of post-training, agent learning and formal reasoning.

An initial research or development direction

An example starting point is to study how training on one recurring reasoning process, such as proof repair or contract refinement, changes performance on new tasks. Strong unadapted baselines and controlled comparisons will establish where the learning method adds value and guide further model development.

Essential background

  • Substantial hands-on experience training or adapting machine-learning models, including fine-tuning or closely related post-training work.
  • Strong implementation and experimental skills, with the ability to diagnose training behaviour, evaluate alternatives and make reproducible improvements.
  • Ability to lead a model-development project from task and data design through training, evaluation and analysis.
  • Relevant technical training or equivalent professional experience. A PhD is not a prerequisite for this engineering profile; formal appointment eligibility will be specified in the final call.

Additional relevant experience

  • Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, agent training, proof or program synthesis, or learning from search and repeated feedback.
  • Distributed training, efficient fine-tuning, experiment management and data pipelines.
  • Formal methods, dependent type theory or interaction with proof assistants. These are useful additions, not entry requirements.

R1-P:
Your role

You will develop formal foundations for agents that act, use resources and delegate authority under explicit commitments. This raises questions that extend beyond the verification of one implementation: how should contracts describe evolving interactions, what does it mean for commitments to compose, and which guarantees can survive changes in state or a transfer of responsibility to another agent? The position offers an opportunity to shape that scientific agenda.

You will develop an independent line of research connecting foundational theory and mechanized reasoning. The agenda spans dependent type theory, semantics, compositional verification, resource representations and their connections to executable systems. These themes offer substantial research directions for both foundational and implementation-oriented researchers. You will establish a focused contribution within this wider programme, working with a team whose expertise covers complementary parts of the agenda.

Within PC2, the research encompasses extensions to the contract calculus and methods for representing domains, resources and tool effects so that admissible actions can be characterised precisely. Questions include reasoning about contractual state, obligations and authority, preserving commitments through delegation, and connecting tool behaviour to the evidence needed before an action can proceed. The objective is reusable specification and verification methods connecting expressive domain models with tractable guarantees.

You will collaborate with systems and learning researchers to explore how these formal choices affect execution and proof generation. Research directions include compositional rules with mechanized guarantees, resource representations that simplify reasoning, and abstractions that transfer between domains. Filesystem access, messaging and payment-like operations provide contrasting domains for developing and evaluating these methods. As the work matures, there will be opportunities to help steward public specifications and formal libraries.

Your contribution to the field

Your contribution will strengthen the mathematical foundations of agents that act under contracts. The agenda connects new calculi, compositional rules, resource abstractions and mechanized results to emerging questions about autonomous action and delegation. By developing reusable specification and verification methods, you will establish an independent line of research with relevance beyond PC2 and help shape the formal interfaces on which other researchers and agent systems build.

An initial research or development direction

An example starting point is to investigate a contract-composition or tool-semantics question through a precise model and a central theoretical or mechanized result, then examine its implications in a small executable case. Foundational analysis and reusable proof infrastructure provide complementary routes into this agenda.

Essential background

  • A PhD in computer science, mathematics or a closely related field; the required stage of completion and formal eligibility will be specified in the final call.
  • Research experience in formal methods and dependent type theory, through foundational work, formal specification, mechanization or verification research.
  • Ability to develop precise definitions and rigorous arguments, and communicate a research contribution clearly.
  • Interest in connecting formal foundations to agent interaction, resources or tool use. Complementary strengths in theory and practical formalization are valued.

Additional relevant experience

  • Compositional verification, programming-language semantics, resource-sensitive reasoning, protocol verification or automated reasoning.
  • Experience with Lean, Rocq/Coq, Agda or other proof-assistant environments; no particular assistant is a universal entry requirement.
  • Reusable formal libraries, proof automation, verified interfaces or research software development.

Candidates with depth in a relevant area and an interest in connecting it to others are encouraged to apply. Evidence of your contribution can include research papers, formal developments, substantial software or a clear account of technical work that cannot be shared publicly.

The role requires close collaboration with the other participating groups, including opportunities for extended visiting periods at their laboratories, bringing your work into close contact with complementary expertise in machine learning, formal methods and systems.

The position is based in Turin, Italy. Remote working arrangements can be agreed when working from another laboratory in the PC2 collaboration. The timing and practical arrangements for research visits will be discussed with you and the participating hosts.

Computational resources. AI4I's HPC infrastructure provides approximately 150 NVIDIA GPUs (80 Blackwell B200 and 68 Hopper H200) and 5 PB of storage, supporting this project in agentic AI training, testing and validation.

You will be expected and supported to lead original research and publish in conferences and journals relevant to formal methods, programming languages, logic and AI. Projects will be developed jointly with your supervisor while preserving an identifiable contribution and room for independent ideas. R2:
Your role

You will investigate how human intent can become a trustworthy basis for autonomous action. When requirements are incomplete or ambiguous, producing a precise specification is only part of the problem: it is also essential to establish whether it captures the decisions and restrictions that matter to the people it represents. The position offers a research agenda at the boundary of AI and formal methods, centred on specification, reasoning and validation.

You will develop new foundations and methods for learning-based specification: how should a system represent competing interpretations, discover what is missing, and use interaction to improve its understanding? The agenda brings together formal analysis, synthesis, algorithms and empirical investigation, with distinct research questions across these areas. The position offers scope for theoretically oriented formal-methods research as well as learning-based systems, with ownership of an identifiable research direction.

Within PC2, these questions arise when agents turn informal requirements into candidate contracts and actively test their meaning. Research directions include clarification, example- and counterexample-guided synthesis, and adversarial specification testing: searching for behaviour that satisfies a written contract but conflicts with the intended requirement. Such interactions can reveal unintended permissions, unnecessary restrictions or choices that require further input from the principal.

You will work with the ML research engineer to develop and train agents that improve at these processes, and with the calculus researchers on their formal representations. The agenda includes selecting informative clarification questions, using feedback from counterexamples and learning across repeated refinement. Evaluation will distinguish formal acceptance from fidelity to intended requirements, with realistic and held-out cases developed alongside the empirical team. Prior expertise in large-scale model training or a specific proof assistant is not required.

Your contribution to the field

Your contribution will advance intent contractualization as a research area connecting formal specification, synthesis and learning. You will develop methods for exposing ambiguity, testing the consequences of alternative specifications and using interaction to refine contracts, together with evidence about their fidelity to intended requirements. The resulting algorithms, formal analyses and evaluation methods will establish a distinctive contribution to how autonomous systems acquire the rules they are expected to follow.

An initial research or development direction

An example starting point is to investigate how counterexamples and targeted questions help an agent resolve ambiguity, comparing an interactive method with direct contractualization. The analysis will examine agreement with independently reviewed requirements, unintended permissions, omissions and review effort.

Essential background

  • A PhD in computer science, mathematics or a closely related field; the required stage of completion and formal eligibility will be specified in the final call.
  • Research experience in formal methods, including dependent type theory and relevant work in specification, synthesis, verification or automated reasoning.
  • Ability to formulate a precise research question and develop rigorous methods or analyses; foundational and implementation-oriented profiles are both welcome.
  • Interest in using learning and interaction to improve specification and reasoning, and in collaborating with researchers developing and training agents.

Additional relevant experience

  • Counterexample-guided methods, program synthesis, interactive specification or formal analysis of requirements.
  • Language models, active learning, agent training or evaluation of generated specifications.
  • Practical proof-assistant or research-software experience. Expertise in Lean is welcome but is not the only relevant background.

Candidates with depth in a relevant area and an interest in connecting it to others are encouraged to apply. Evidence of your contribution can include research papers, formal developments, substantial software or a clear account of technical work that cannot be shared publicly.

R3:
Your role

You will investigate how capable agents can become reliable actors under explicit constraints. The research aims to understand the relationship between learning, planning and verification: can agents use formal feedback to perform more useful work, rather than simply avoid actions that might fail a check? This is an opportunity to develop methods and evidence that shape how safe agentic capabilities are understood and evaluated.

The position offers ownership of an empirical research agenda, with scope to introduce new learning or planning methods and question how progress should be measured. The agenda spans policy-aware planning, proof-generating agents, recovery from failed reasoning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, offering distinct directions for a substantial research contribution.

Within PC2, you will bring these ideas into realistic task environments where agents must satisfy explicit policies while using tools and completing workflows. Working with formal-methods and systems researchers, you will connect those policies to contracts and reusable Airlock integrations. These settings will make it possible to study when verification helps, when it obstructs useful behaviour, and how agent methods can improve the balance.

You will collaborate with the ML research engineer on model development while leading the questions and comparisons behind your studies. Evaluation will distinguish task success, constraint satisfaction, intervention and computational cost, using controlled comparisons, held-out cases and informative negative results. As the programme develops, you will help shape a public benchmark or evaluation resource and engage other researchers in reproducing or challenging its findings.

Your contribution to the field

Your contribution will shape how safe agentic capabilities are learned and evaluated. New planning or learning methods, together with reproducible studies of their performance under explicit policies, will reveal how verification changes useful autonomy and where current approaches fall short. Public evaluation resources and research results will give other teams a basis for comparing agents across tasks, constraints and computational budgets, and establish your own line of work at the intersection of empirical ML and verifiable action.

An initial research or development direction

An example starting point is to test whether an agent trained to anticipate contractual constraints completes more useful work than one that encounters them only after an action is rejected. A realistic task family, credible baselines and controlled comparisons will support the study and guide method development.

Essential background

  • A PhD in machine learning, artificial intelligence, computer science or a closely related field; the required stage of completion and formal eligibility will be specified in the final call.
  • Strong empirical research and implementation skills in machine learning, agent systems, reinforcement learning or a related area.
  • Ability to design controlled experiments, analyse failures and distinguish competing explanations for an observed improvement.
  • Interest in developing agent capabilities under explicit constraints and collaborating with formal-methods and systems researchers.

Additional relevant experience

  • Policy-aware planning, proof-generating agents, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards or learning from tool feedback.
  • Agent benchmarks, realistic task environments, reproducible evaluation or adversarial testing.

R4:
Your role

You will study the foundations of trustworthy cooperation between agents representing different principals. When agents have different information, resources and responsibilities, the behaviour of the network cannot be understood by evaluating each participant in isolation. The position offers an opportunity to investigate how useful collective behaviour can emerge while preserving the commitments under which each agent is authorised to act.

You will shape a research agenda in multi-agent coordination and verifiable delegation, connecting empirical investigation with new interaction protocols, coordination methods or learning-based approaches. Central questions concern how authority should be distributed, how network structure affects cooperation, and how local guarantees relate to system-level outcomes. You will develop a focused line of research within this agenda, shaping its methods and experiments alongside colleagues with complementary expertise.

Within PC2, you will develop and test settings in which agents communicate, use resources and delegate work under explicit contracts. The research settings span central coordination, hierarchical delegation and interaction between separately operated services. You will vary topology, information, resource limits and adversarial behaviour to establish which features change safety or useful completion. You will work with the calculus team on the guarantees being tested and with engineers and empirical researchers on realistic execution.

A central aim is to distinguish failures of enforcement from undesirable outcomes despite contractual compliance, and to understand how either can propagate through an interaction network. The resulting studies will guide method development and identify limits of the current specifications. There will be opportunities to help shape an open multi-agent benchmark or protocol profile and to collaborate with researchers investigating compatible systems.

Your contribution to the field

Your contribution will advance the science of coordination between agents representing different principals. By connecting interaction structure, contractual guarantees and observed network behaviour, you will develop evidence and methods for distributing authority while preserving the commitments that govern a shared task. New coordination approaches, comparative studies and open multi-agent environments will establish a distinctive research contribution to trustworthy delegation across organisational boundaries.

An initial research or development direction

An example starting point is to compare delegation structures on matched tasks with explicit principal-level constraints, identifying which arrangements support useful cooperation and where commitments conflict. The study will test the assumptions needed for local checks to support global behaviour and inform the design of coordination methods.

Essential background

  • A PhD in artificial intelligence, computer science or a closely related field; the required stage of completion and formal eligibility will be specified in the final call.
  • Research experience relevant to multi-agent systems, coordination, planning, distributed AI or rigorous experimentation with interacting agents.
  • Strong implementation and experimental-design skills, and the ability to turn an interaction-level question into a reproducible study.
  • Interest in distinct principals, delegated authority and the relationship between local agent behaviour and system-level outcomes.

Additional relevant experience

  • Multi-agent learning, decentralised planning, negotiation, heterogeneous agents or protocol design.
  • Agent security, collusion or adversarial interactions, realistic benchmarks and analysis of network structure.
  • Formal methods, dependent type theory, compositional guarantees or proof assistants. Prior specialisation in formal methods is not required.
